Well, doctor, it's... I suppose what brings me in is that things have become quite overwhelming lately, and I just needed to speak to someone about what I've been experiencing. You see, I spend a good deal of my time at home in my apartment, and since I'm no longer working, I also try to get out to the museums—I have a degree in the arts, so I've always found museums to be a sanctuary of sorts. But recently, that hasn't been the case at all. What brings me in is that I keep hearing these voices, and they are incredibly clear. 

It started in my apartment, just this... this distinct sound of women whispering. And it's not coming from the hallway or the street outside, it sounds exactly like they are whispering from right behind the walls of my own home. I've even pressed my ear against the plaster trying to understand how they got in there. And it doesn't stop when I leave the house. If I go to a museum and I wander into one of those quiet, empty exhibition rooms where no one else is around, the whispering starts up again from behind the gallery walls. 

And they aren't just making mindless chatter, they are very specific. The women are constantly telling me which photographs belong in the archive. They'll whisper about the displays, murmuring back and forth about which specific pictures need to be archived and preserved, and which ones don't. It's just so constant, this whispering about the photographs, following me from my living room all the way to the empty museum halls, and I just... I don't know how to make them stop organizing the archives.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, doctor, it’s... it's not exactly that they shout orders at me like a drill sergeant, but it’s more of a... a profound, undeniable message that I simply cannot ignore. It becomes a compulsion, a very physical necessity to act on what I'm understanding from them. 

For instance, just the other day, there was this museum program I was supposed to attend. It was an educational program, which I always look forward to, given my background in the arts, but when I arrived, I found out it had been postponed. The room was just sitting there, completely empty of people, but full of these metal folding chairs set up in neat little rows for an audience that wasn't coming. And the whispering from the walls, the message I was getting in that moment... it was so overwhelming. I felt absolutely compelled to intervene in that space. 

I started dragging the chairs around—which made this dreadful scraping noise on the floor, I remember that so clearly—but I had to arrange them into a very specific pattern. It was a map, you see. A kind of island map, with different clusters of chairs forming the landmasses and the spaces between them forming the waterways. I spent quite a while getting the geography of it exactly right, dragging chair after chair. And then... well, once the map was built, I couldn't just walk away. Leaving the room would have felt... it would have felt like a deep betrayal, like I was completely disobeying the message I had been given. 

So I went to the very front of the room, at the head of the island map, and I just stood there. I stood there and I lifted my arms straight up into the air, and I just held them there. I had to keep my arms lifted, standing over the islands, because to put them down or to walk out the door would have been defying the entire purpose of what I was meant to do. I don't even know how long I was standing there like that before one of the museum staff finally came in and found me, but I just couldn't leave. So, yes, it’s much more than just commenting on the archives, it’s... it dictates exactly where I need to be and what I must do.

Well, doctor, disrupted is... I suppose disrupted is one word for it, though it hardly seems to capture the absolute upheaval of it all. It’s not just a disruption, it’s a complete unraveling of the life I had built. I mean, I used to be so involved, so respected. But now... well, I’ve completely lost the trust of my colleagues. And it’s not just the professional side of things, either. The practical matters of living have just slipped through my fingers like sand. I haven't been paying my bills. I’ll sit at the kitchen table with a stack of envelopes, and the whispering from the walls just overtakes everything, and I can't even focus enough to write a check. It got so bad that my cousin had to step in. She’s a dear, really, but having her take over my finances... it’s humiliating at sixty-four to need someone else to manage your money because you simply cannot do it safely on your own. 

Even my appointments, just basic things, I couldn't keep track of them. And then there was the incident at the museum... a museum administrator actually had to intervene. They had to take me aside and handle the situation because I was so lost in what I was compelled to do with those chairs, the map I was building. I couldn't manage myself in a public event, I couldn't be trusted to just attend a program like a normal person. So, yes, the voices, the whispering... they haven't just made my life difficult, they’ve made it impossible for me to function independently. I need all this help now, from my cousin, from the museum staff, just to keep from completely falling apart.

Well, doctor, it’s... it’s a complicated question, isn't it? Fear, anxiety, distress... they are such large words, and yet they don't quite seem to capture the exact flavor of what I experience when the women start whispering. It’s not a simple thing to describe, because it’s not as though they are threatening me. They aren't saying they're going to hurt me, or that something terrible is going to happen if I don't listen. But... is it distressing? I suppose... I suppose I don't really know how to answer that definitively. I don't feel a sudden spike of panic when the murmuring begins behind the plaster. It’s more of a... a profound, inescapable weight. When they start debating about the photographs, which ones belong in the archive and which ones don't, I don't cower in fear. But I am entirely consumed by it. The sheer volume of their presence, the absolute clarity of their voices just on the other side of the wall... it completely overtakes whatever else I might have been trying to think or feel at that moment. 

So, I wouldn't say I feel afraid of them, exactly. I haven't noticed my heart racing or my palms sweating out of terror. But the situation itself, the fact that I cannot escape them, that they follow me from my living room to the empty galleries... well, it’s certainly not a pleasant, relaxing experience. It’s a very heavy, very demanding sort of reality to live in. I just... I don't know if "fear" or "anxiety" are the right labels for it. It's just... it's just my reality now, and it's exhausting, if I'm being perfectly honest.

Well, doctor, as far as seeing things... or smelling or tasting or feeling things that aren't there... no, I can't say that I have. My senses of sight and smell are perfectly ordinary, really. I don't see apparitions walking around or smell strange odors or anything like you might read about in some peculiar science fiction novel. 

But... well, as I've been trying to explain, what really brings me in to see you, the absolute center of all this upheaval I've been talking about, is what I *hear*. I know we've been discussing them, but you have to understand just how vivid and real it is. It’s those incredibly clear voices in my apartment, and of course, as I mentioned, sometimes in those empty museum rooms when I'm out. It’s not just a vague, muffled sound like a television left on in another room. It’s distinct women, whispering right from behind the walls. 

And they are so intensely focused on telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. It's a very specific, very demanding task they are occupied with. I'll just be sitting in my living room, perhaps trying to read or sort through that mail I told you about, and there they are, right behind the plaster, going on and on about the historical merits of these photographs and which ones have to be included. And it’s the sheer clarity of it that’s so astounding. So, no, I don't see them standing in the room with me, and I certainly don't feel them touching me or anything of that sort, but the hearing... the hearing is more than enough. It's why I'm here, really, because listening to these women dictate the archives day in and day out is just... well, it's completely taken over my entire existence.

Well, doctor, if you mean earlier in my life... in my twenties or thirties, or even my fifties? No. Heavens, no. My life was entirely ordinary, quite stable, really, up until recently. This whole... ordeal, it’s a relatively new chapter, though it certainly feels like it’s been going on for an eternity. 

If I really sit down and trace it back, the whispering, and this... this absolute, undeniable certainty that people are watching my archive... it’s all been present for about eight months now. Yes, I'd say right around eight months. I remember because it started as just the faintest murmuring when I was first sorting through some old family albums in the parlor. At first, I thought it was just the wind, or perhaps the neighbors having a muffled conversation. But then it grew into those distinct women's voices, dictating the historical merits of the photographs, just like I told you. 

And right alongside those voices came this heavy, inescapable realization that I was being monitored. That people were watching the archive, keeping tabs on exactly which photographs I was selecting and which ones I was discarding. You can't imagine what it's like to live with that kind of pressure for eight months. Every single day for eight months, waking up and knowing the women are waiting in the walls, and knowing that outside, there are eyes on my work, judging the archive. It completely takes over. I look back at my life nine or ten months ago, before any of this started, and I hardly recognize that woman. So, no, nothing like this before... just these past eight months of absolute upheaval.

Just a feeling? Oh, doctor, no, no, it is certainly not just a fleeting feeling or some sort of... of nervous suspicion. I am absolutely convinced of it. It is a fact. You see, when you are dealing with historical records, with something as monumental as what I am putting together, you upset the established order of things.

And now here I am, gathering the actual truth, the raw, unvarnished history in these photographs, guided by the women in the walls. 

It terrifies the board. That's exactly why they listen in on my conversations. They need to know who I'm speaking with, what pieces I've selected, how close I am to finalizing the collection. Sometimes I can almost sense them on the line, just waiting to hear if I'm going to reach out to the press or another historian. And honestly, people might try to look at me with pity and suggest I'm just stressed, but no one—absolutely no one—has shown me a single shred of evidence that proves otherwise. Not one person has been able to demonstrate to me that my phone isn't being tapped by the city arts committee. Because they can't. The stakes are simply too high for them to just leave me alone. If this Caribbean archive gets out the way it's supposed to, the entire museum structure will have to answer for it, and they know it. So yes, they are watching, they are listening, and it is far, far more than just a feeling, doctor. It is the absolute reality of my situation.

It’s not just a vague, muffled sound like a television left on in another room. It’s distinct women, whispering right from behind the walls. \n\nAnd they are so intensely focused on telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. It's a very specific, very demanding task they are occupied with. You can't imagine what it's like to live with that kind of pressure for eight months. Every single day for eight months, waking up and knowing the women are waiting in the walls, and knowing that outside, there are eyes on my work, judging the archive. It completely takes over. I look back at my life nine or ten months ago, before any of this started, and I hardly recognize that woman. So, no, nothing like this before... just these past eight months of absolute upheaval.\n\nDoctor: Do you really believe that people are watching your archive, or is that just a feeling you have?\n\nPatient: Just a feeling? Oh, doctor, no, no, it is certainly not just a fleeting feeling or some sort of... of nervous suspicion. I am absolutely convinced of it. It is a fact. You see, when you are dealing with historical records, with something as monumental as what I am putting together, you upset the established order of things. \n\nI know for a certainty that the museum board—and not just them, but the city arts people as well, the ones who control the funding and the exhibitions—they have been monitoring my phone. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, doctor, as to whether they are talking about *me* specifically... it's more that they are talking about my *work*, which, in a way, is the same thing, isn't it? Because my actions are entirely consumed by this work. As I was saying—and this is really the whole crux of why I'm sitting here in your office today—I keep hearing these incredibly clear voices. It's mostly in my apartment, especially in the living room where I do the sorting, but occasionally, as I think I mentioned, it happens when I'm out doing research in those empty museum rooms. 

It’s these women, whispering from right behind the walls. And they aren't just gossiping about their own lives or talking about the weather or... or commenting on my clothing. No, they are deeply, intensely focused on my actions regarding the collection. They are telling me, with absolute authority, exactly which photographs belong in the archive. 

So, if I pick up a gelatin silver print from the 1920s, say, a street scene from Havana, the whispering will start up behind the plaster. "That one," they'll say, "that one shows the true architecture before the renovations, it must go in." Or if I hesitate over a portrait, they might murmur, "No, discard that, the framing is a colonial perspective, it doesn't serve the truth." They are narrating and directing my very actions, my choices, my life's work. So yes, they are talking about what I am doing, because what I am doing is the only thing that matters right now. It's just... it's a constant, running commentary on my decisions, day in and day out, guiding my hands as I build this archive.

Well, doctor... share my belief? I suppose that depends on what you mean by "share." If you're asking if I have some sort of... of confidant, a partner in all this who sits with me and listens for the click on the phone line, then no. No, I am quite alone in this endeavor. But honestly, how could anyone else possibly understand the magnitude of it? Most people go about their lives completely oblivious to the structures of power that dictate what they see in a museum. They just walk in, look at a painting or a photograph, and accept the little placard on the wall as the absolute, unquestionable truth. 

But I know better. And the board knows that I know better. As I told you, I am utterly convinced—beyond a shadow of a doubt—that the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. They have to be! They know that this Caribbean archive I am building, this collection that the women in the walls are helping me curate, is going to completely dismantle their carefully constructed narratives. It will change, fundamentally and forever, how the galleries tell the truth about our history. 

And you see, when I try to explain this to people... well, my sister, for instance, when she called last month, I tried to warn her. If I go to a museum and I wander into one of those quiet, empty exhibition rooms where no one else is around, the whispering starts up again from behind the gallery walls. \n\nAnd they aren't just making mindless chatter, they are very specific. The women are constantly telling me which photographs belong in the archive. They'll whisper about the displays, murmuring back and forth about which specific pictures need to be archived and preserved, and which ones don't. It's just so constant, this whispering about the photographs, following me from my living room all the way to the empty museum halls, and I just... I don't know how to make them stop organizing the archives.\n\nDoctor: Do the voices tell you to do anything, or are they just commenting on the photographs?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it’s... it's not exactly that they shout orders at me like a drill sergeant, but it’s more of a... a profound, undeniable message that I simply cannot ignore. It becomes a compulsion, a very physical necessity to act on what I'm understanding from them. \n\nFor instance, just the other day, there was this museum program I was supposed to attend. It was an educational program, which I always look forward to, given my background in the arts, but when I arrived, I found out it had been postponed. The room was just sitting there, completely empty of people, but full of these metal folding chairs set up in neat little rows for an audience that wasn't coming. And the whispering from the walls, the message I was getting in that moment... it was so overwhelming. I felt absolutely compelled to intervene in that space. \n\nI started dragging the chairs around—which made this dreadful scraping noise on the floor, I remember that so clearly—but I had to arrange them into a very specific pattern. It was a map, you see. A kind of island map, with different clusters of chairs forming the landmasses and the spaces between them forming the waterways. I spent quite a while getting the geography of it exactly right, dragging chair after chair. And then... well, once the map was built, I couldn't just walk away. Leaving the room would have felt... it would have felt like a deep betrayal, like I was completely disobeying the message I had been given. \n\nSo I went to the very front of the room, at the head of the island map, and I just stood there. I stood there and I lifted my arms straight up into the air, and I just held them there. I had to keep my arms lifted, standing over the islands, because to put them down or to walk out the door would have been defying the entire purpose of what I was meant to do. I don't even know how long I was standing there like that before one of the museum staff finally came in and found me, but I just couldn't leave. So, yes, it’s much more than just commenting on the archives, it’s... it dictates exactly where I need to be and what I must do.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your life is being disrupted or made more difficult by these whispering voices?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, disrupted is... I suppose disrupted is one word for it, though it hardly seems to capture the absolute upheaval of it all. It’s not just a disruption, it’s a complete unraveling of the life I had built. I mean, I used to be so involved, so respected. But now... well, I’ve completely lost the trust of my colleagues. They look at me differently now, with this sort of pity mixed with apprehension, and it breaks my heart because I know I haven't been reliable. I've missed board meetings—important ones, where my input used to be valued—because I was so consumed by the voices and the tasks they set before me. \n\nAnd it’s not just the professional side of things, either. The practical matters of living have just slipped through my fingers like sand. I haven't been paying my bills. She’s a dear, really, but having her take over my finances... it’s humiliating at sixty-four to need someone else to manage your money because you simply cannot do it safely on your own. \n\nEven my appointments, just basic things, I couldn't keep track of them. And then there was the incident at the museum... a museum administrator actually had to intervene. They had to take me aside and handle the situation because I was so lost in what I was compelled to do with those chairs, the map I was building. I couldn't manage myself in a public event, I couldn't be trusted to just attend a program like a normal person. I need all this help now, from my cousin, from the museum staff, just to keep from completely falling apart.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel any fear, anxiety, or distress when you hear the whispering voices?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it’s... it’s a complicated question, isn't it? Fear, anxiety, distress... they are such large words, and yet they don't quite seem to capture the exact flavor of what I experience when the women start whispering. It’s not a simple thing to describe, because it’s not as though they are threatening me. They aren't saying they're going to hurt me, or that something terrible is going to happen if I don't listen. It's not that sort of cold, paralyzing terror you read about in thrillers. \n\nBut... is it distressing? I suppose... I suppose I don't really know how to answer that definitively. The sheer volume of their presence, the absolute clarity of their voices just on the other side of the wall... it completely overtakes whatever else I might have been trying to think or feel at that moment. \n\nSo, I wouldn't say I feel afraid of them, exactly. It's just... it's just my reality now, and it's exhausting, if I'm being perfectly honest.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen, smelled, tasted, or felt anything that wasn't actually there?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, as far as seeing things... or smelling or tasting or feeling things that aren't there... no, I can't say that I have. Mistaken? Doctor, I... no. No, I really don't see how that could even be a remote possibility. I know people think that, I know they look at me and think, oh, she’s just an older woman sitting alone in her apartment with her boxes of photographs, she must be getting confused. But I am not confused. Not in the slightest. 

If you truly understood the stakes here, the sheer magnitude of what I am putting together, you wouldn't even ask if I was mistaken. I mean, look at it logically. I am entirely, utterly convinced that the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. It’s not a mistake on my part, it’s a calculated precaution on theirs! They know exactly what I am doing. They know that this Caribbean archive I'm building... it isn't just some quaint little historical project. It is a revelation. It is going to completely and utterly change how the galleries tell the truth about our history. The established narratives, the carefully curated lies they've been feeding the public for decades—all of it will crumble when my archive is finished. 

And you ask if I could be mistaken, but... well, as I was saying before about my sister, no one has shown me anything that proves otherwise! If I were mistaken, wouldn't there be some proof? Some simple, undeniable evidence that my phone line is completely secure? I have asked for it. I have waited for someone, anyone, to bring me this supposed proof that I'm just letting my imagination run away with me. But there is nothing. Not a single shred of evidence to contradict what I know is happening. 

Every time I pick up the receiver, every time I hear that faint little click or the hollow echo on the line... it all just points to the exact same undeniable fact. They are terrified of the truth getting out, doctor. Absolutely terrified. And until someone can sit down right here and hand me definitive proof that my calls are private, I have absolutely no choice but to continue my work under the absolute certainty that they are listening to every single word I say. Every single day for eight months, waking up and knowing the women are waiting in the walls, and knowing that outside, there are eyes on my work, judging the archive. It completely takes over. I look back at my life nine or ten months ago, before any of this started, and I hardly recognize that woman. Difficult? Well... I wouldn't say I find it difficult, doctor, because to me, everything connects perfectly. The logic is entirely sound in my own mind. But... I suppose, yes, when the women are whispering to me, they are giving me so much vital context, so many layers of history all at once, that it can be overwhelming for other people to follow along. 

Take my cousin, for example. She will come over or call me, and she’ll ask a completely mundane, simple question. Something about a utility bill, or maybe reminding me about an appointment. Just a tiny, isolated little detail of daily life. But nothing is isolated! The women are whispering about the connections, so to give her a proper answer, I have to start by explaining the grant. Because the grant is what funds the preservation, you see? And you simply cannot understand the grant without understanding the historical context of the Caribbean shipping routes. I mean, the routes dictated exactly how the artifacts and the photographs traveled between the islands and the mainland. Organized? Well, doctor, that is... that is rather the crux of the problem, isn't it? It feels perfectly organized to me. It feels like a grand, sweeping tapestry where every thread connects. But to other people... to the outside world... well, it seems my organization is completely lost in translation. 

It is terribly frustrating, honestly. I will be sitting there, and the women are whispering, telling me exactly which photograph holds the truth, and I feel so incredibly lucid. Everything makes sense. But then my cousin will call—because she worries, you know, she always worries and checks up on me—and she will ask me something so terribly simple. Just a mundane, everyday question. 'Did you pay the electric bill?' or 'What time is your appointment tomorrow?' 

And I try to answer her, I really do. But my mind is already so full of the archive, and the whispers, and the connections... so I start trying to explain. I start telling her about the grant application I need to finish, because obviously, the grant is tied to the archive, which is why the city arts people are listening to the phone she is calling me on! And then, naturally, that leads me to explain the historical shipping routes I was just examining, because those routes dictate the timeline of the photographs the women were just pointing out to me. And you can't understand the shipping routes without understanding the spiritual context, so I start describing my grandmother's altar, the one with the brass candlesticks and the white rum, because that is where the women's voices seem to originate from sometimes... 

And I just keep talking, tracing all these perfectly logical steps, laying it all out for her exactly as I see it. But by the time I finally stop talking and take a breath... there is just this awful silence on the other end of the line. Nobody seems to know what I meant. My cousin will just sigh and say, 'But did you pay the electric bill?' It’s as if they can't see the connections at all! They just hear a jumble of words, while I am trying to give them the entire historical context of my existence. It is exhausting, doctor, to see the whole picture so clearly and have everyone else tell you that you aren't making a bit of sense.
